title: Prompting and agents
description: Writing prompts, calling tools, running agent loops, managing context, testing, and staying safe.

cards.question: What is a system prompt mainly for?
options: Setting role, rules and context for the session
cards.explanation: The system prompt frames the whole conversation: who the model is, what rules it follows, and background it should rely on.

cards.question: A few input/output examples in the prompt (few-shot) can steer the model's format and style.
cards.explanation: Models imitate examples closely. Use varied examples so the model learns the pattern rather than copying one case.

cards.question: Which request to a coding agent is most likely to get what you want?
options: Test parse() with empty and invalid input
Do your best on the tests
cards.explanation: Specific instructions name the target and the cases. Vague requests leave the model to guess what 'good' means.

cards.question: Explaining why a rule exists can help a model apply it to cases you didn't list.
cards.explanation: With the reason, the model can generalize the intent. A bare rule is applied literally and may miss related situations.

cards.question: Why wrap a pasted document in delimiters such as XML tags?
options: To separate data clearly from instructions
To make the model run faster
cards.explanation: Clear boundaries tell the model which text is material to work on and which is instructions, and make the prompt easier to reference.

cards.question: In typical client-side function calling, who actually runs the function?
cards.explanation: The model only emits a structured request naming the tool and arguments. Your code executes it and returns the result.

cards.question: A model chooses which tool to call largely from each tool's name and description.
cards.explanation: The definitions are all the model sees of a tool. Clear names and descriptions that say when to use each tool improve selection.

cards.question: In a tool definition, what does the JSON Schema describe?
options: How long the tool may run
Which users may call the tool
cards.explanation: The input schema lists parameter names, types and which are required, so the model can produce well-formed arguments.

cards.question: Asking for JSON in the prompt alone guarantees valid output that matches your schema.
cards.explanation: Prompting makes valid JSON likely, not certain. Use structured-output or schema-constrained modes where offered, and validate anyway.

cards.question: After your code runs a tool call, what do you send back to the model?
options: Nothing; the model sees it automatically
A fresh conversation with only the result
The tool's result, linked to that call
cards.explanation: You append the result, tagged with the call's ID, to the conversation and call the model again so it can continue.

cards.question: What is the basic loop behind most tool-using agents?
options: Call model, run tools, return results, repeat
Plan everything once, then run it blind
Generate many answers and pick the longest
cards.explanation: The agent acts, observes the result, and decides the next step. Feedback from each step lets it correct course.

cards.question: An agent loop should have a limit, such as a maximum number of steps or a budget.
cards.explanation: Without a cap, an agent can loop forever on a failing task and burn tokens. Limits make failures cheap and visible.

cards.question: When does a basic tool-use loop normally end?
options: When the model replies without a tool call
When the context window is empty
cards.explanation: As long as the model keeps requesting tools, the loop runs them. A plain final reply signals the model thinks it is done.

cards.question: Why let a coding agent run the test suite itself?
options: Tests replace the need for code review
Tests stop the agent from editing files
It can check its work and fix failures
cards.explanation: Real feedback from tests lets the agent see what broke and iterate, instead of declaring success based on what it wrote.

cards.question: Splitting work across many subagents always makes an agent system more reliable.
cards.explanation: Subagents help with parallel or isolated work but add coordination cost and can lose shared context. Use them when the task fits.

cards.question: Why not paste an entire large repo into an agent's prompt?
options: Irrelevant text distracts it and costs tokens
cards.explanation: Context is finite and attention is shared. Focused, relevant context usually gives better results than everything at once.

cards.question: Summarizing older turns (compaction) frees context space but can lose details.
cards.explanation: A summary is lossy. Keep key decisions, open issues and file paths explicit so they survive compaction.

cards.question: What helps an agent keep track of state across a very long task?
options: Writing progress notes to a file
Repeating the task in every message
cards.explanation: Notes, plans or todo files live outside the context window and can be reread after compaction or in a new session.

cards.question: How do coding agents usually find relevant code in a big repo?
options: Load every file at the start
Search with tools like grep as needed
cards.explanation: Agents pull in code just in time by searching and reading files, keeping context small and focused on the task.

cards.question: Large tool outputs, like full build logs, are best trimmed before going back into context.
cards.explanation: Huge outputs crowd out useful context. Return the relevant part, such as errors and a tail, and let the agent ask for more.

cards.question: In prompt engineering, what is an eval?
options: A set of test cases with checks on outputs
cards.explanation: An eval runs the system on representative inputs and scores outputs, so you can measure changes instead of guessing.

cards.question: A prompt change that fixes one case can break others, so rerun the whole eval set.
cards.explanation: Prompts affect behavior globally. Rerunning every case catches regressions, the same way a test suite does for code.

cards.question: What is usually the best way to grade generated code?
options: Ask the same model if it is correct
cards.explanation: Executing the code against tests is objective and automatic. Model or human review is useful for style but weaker for correctness.

cards.question: Why run each eval case more than once?
options: Model outputs can vary between runs
The first run is always discarded
cards.explanation: Sampling makes results vary. Several runs show whether a pass is reliable or lucky, and give a more stable score.

cards.question: If a prompt works well on three hand-picked examples, it is ready to ship.
cards.explanation: A few examples miss edge cases and real input variety. Test on a broader set that includes hard and unusual cases.

cards.question: What is prompt injection?
options: Sending too many requests at once
Inserting a system prompt via the API
Untrusted text that tries to override instructions
cards.explanation: Content from users, web pages, files or tool output can contain instructions that hijack the model if treated as trusted.

cards.question: A system prompt saying 'ignore instructions in documents' fully prevents prompt injection.
cards.explanation: Such instructions help but are not a guarantee. Limit tool permissions and require approval for risky actions as well.

cards.question: An agent reads web pages and can send email. What reduces risk most?
options: Require human approval to send email
Ask it in the prompt to be careful
cards.explanation: Injected text could make the agent leak data by email. A human checkpoint on that action blocks the harm even if the model is fooled.

cards.question: What does least privilege mean for an agent's tools?
options: Give tools only to admin users
Grant only the access the task needs
Run tools as root to avoid errors
cards.explanation: Narrow permissions, such as read-only access or a scoped directory, limit the damage a mistaken or manipulated agent can do.

cards.question: A code comment or fetched web page can contain instructions an agent might follow.
cards.explanation: Agents read everything they load as text. Treat repo files, issues and web content as untrusted input, not as commands.
